title: Data Collection Facts Label
text:
Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), 2023 National High School Dataset, part of CDC’s Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS)




Domain/topic


Public and adolescent health. It covers health behaviors, experiences, and conditions of high school students, including social media use frequency, bullying, mental health, sleep, and substance use.




Source type


Government dataset. It is public, published by a U.S. federal agency, and downloadable with documentation.











Collection Context






Collector/producer


CDC’s Division of Adolescent and School Health (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion), a public federal agency. ICF served as the survey contractor. The CDC and ICF institutional review boards approved the protocol.




Original purpose


The YRBSS started in 1991 to keep track of health risk behaviors in U.S. high school students. The CDC wanted to see how common these behaviors are, how they change over time, and how they overlap, plus keep an eye on Healthy People goals. It also grew to track experiences and conditions that affect health. In 2023 the CDC added new questions, social media included, to get national data on newer topics.




Collection method


Students took the survey on tablets during one class period. It was anonymous and voluntary. The tablets weren’t connected to the internet, so data collectors synced everything to a central spot at the end of each day. Students who were absent could take a web version when they came back (323 did). Local parent permission rules were followed, and it was offered in English and Spanish. Schools were picked with a three-stage cluster sample: counties first, then schools, then classrooms.




Record-creation event


A student in a picked classroom finishes the questionnaire. The record stays in the data if it passes quality control.











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


One student. One finished questionnaire is one row.




Population or objects represented


Students in grades 9 to 12 at public (charter included) and private schools in the 50 states and D.C. Left out of the school list: alternative schools, special education schools, Department of Defense schools, Bureau of Indian Education schools, vocational schools where students also attend another school, and schools with 40 or fewer students in grades 9 to 12. The CDC says homeschooled students and students not in school aren’t represented. In 2023 they added an extra American Indian/Alaska Native sample, and Black and Hispanic students were oversampled.




Time period covered


Spring semester (January to June) 2023. The survey happens every two years, and 2023 was the first year with a social media question.




Geographic area coverage


The whole U.S. (50 states and D.C.). 155 schools took part. The data is weighted so it represents U.S. high schoolers overall.











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Age (Q1, 12 or younger up to 18 or older), sex, grade, race and ethnicity, self-reported height and weight, BMI, how often they use social media (Q80, 8 options from not at all to more than once an hour), bullied at school (Q24), electronically bullied (Q25), sad or hopeless (Q26), suicide questions (Q27 to Q29), poor mental health (Q84), sleep (Q85), grades (Q87), questions on tobacco, alcohol, drugs, sex, diet, and exercise, a yes/no version of every question (QN#), and the survey design variables WEIGHT, STRATUM, and PSU.




Data types included


Mostly categorical. Multiple choice answers are saved as codes, and a lot of them are frequency scales. Race (Q5) lets you pick more than one. Height and weight were typed in, then converted to meters and kilograms. BMI and BMI percentile are calculated numbers. WEIGHT is numeric, PSU and STRATUM are design codes, and the QN# variables are 1 for yes and 2 for no. I didn’t find any free text, images, GPS, audio, or sensor data in the documentation.




Direct measurements


Everything is a survey answer with no sensors or physical measurements, so the directly recorded items are things students reported like age, sex, grade, height and weight, how often they use social media, yes/no on bullying, and hours of sleep on a school night.




Possible proxy variables


The CDC doesn’t label any variable a proxy, but ones to look at in the next phase are Q80 for overall social media use (it doesn’t ask which app, what they do on it, or how long), Q26 and Q84 for depression, anxiety, or wellbeing, Q25 for online harassment, and the BMI, overweight, and obese flags that are calculated from self-reported height and weight.











Documentation






Documentation found


The 2023 YRBS Data User’s Guide with the codebook (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/media/pdf/2023/2023_National_YRBS_Data_Users_Guide508.pdf), the CDC methods report by Brener et al. (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/su/su7304a1.htm), the CDC social media report by Young et al. (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/su/su7304a3.htm), the 2023 questionnaire (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/questionnaires/index.html), SAS and SPSS programs for reading the data (https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/data/index.html), and the online tools Youth Online (https://nccd.cdc.gov/Youthonline/App/Default.aspx), YRBS Analysis Tool (https://yrbs-analysis.cdc.gov), and YRBS Explorer (https://yrbs-explorer.services.cdc.gov).




Stated collection details


20,386 questionnaires were finished in 155 schools and 20,103 passed quality control, with response rates of 49.8% for schools, 71.0% for students, and 35.4% overall, missing data wasn’t filled in with estimates, the weights adjust for nonresponse and oversampling, not every student got every question (so how many answered each one changes, and 4,900 are missing on the social media question), the CDC cites a test-retest study showing most questions were reliable, it’s a cross-sectional survey, and the CDC doesn’t state why individual schools or students declined.

text:
Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


National, state, and district Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS)




Domain/topic


Health




Source type


Government Dataset











Collection Context






Collector/producer


CDC, Government Agency




Original purpose


The data was taken to track leading behaviors and experiences that contribute to leading causes of death in adolescents and adults in the united states




Collection method


A survey given to 9th - 12th graders




Record-creation event


Taking a survey











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


A person, each column representing a survey response




Population or objects represented


9th - 12th graders in public schools across the united states




Time period covered


Survey is taken every 2 years, this specific one is from 2025




Geographic area coverage


The United States











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Age, Sex, Race




Data types included


Categorical, Numerical, Text (free response fields)




Direct measurements


Age, Sex, Race, height, weight, social media use time




Possible proxy variables


We can likely use self harm, feelings of hopelessness, and suicidal ideations as proxies for depression, since those are all typical symptoms.











Documentation






Documentation found


User’s Guide PDF




Stated collection details


Not Stated

title: analysis
text:
The source that best seems to fit our research question of “How does social media affect behavior?” is the 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey dataset(YRBS). We only had two datasets to choose from, but they ended up being from the same source, just different years. Both the 2023 and 2025 datasets come from the CDC, making them trustworthy sources with plenty of documentation on how the data was collected. While the 2023 dataset has a larger sample size of 20,103 students compared to 10,710 in 2025, along with a higher response rate, we chose 2025 because it provides more recent information on high school students and their social media habits. The smaller sample size and lower response rate in 2025 could mean that certain groups of students are less represented, which is something we have to consider when analyzing the data.
Both datasets collect information through anonymous surveys, which helps protect students privacy, especially when asking about sensitive topics like mental health and bullying. However, since students report their own answers, there is a possibility of inaccurate responses or bias. For example, some students might not feel comfortable answering questions about their mental health or personal experiences truthfully. Another limitation is that neither dataset includes students who are homeschooled or not attending school, meaning they don’t represent all teenagers. Even though both datasets are meant to represent high school students across the United States, there are still groups that aren’t included.
Both datasets also measure how frequently students use social media, but don’t really show what they’re doing on these platforms or how much time they spend on them. This limits what we can conclude about how social media affects behavior, since someone who frequently uses social media to communicate with friends might have different experiences than someone who mainly scrolls through content. We would also be using things like bullying, sleep, and mental health responses to help understand behavior, even though these don’t capture every aspect of it. If we could improve the 2025 dataset, we would add questions about specific platforms, time spent using them, and the type of content students interact with.
Overall, we believe the 2025 dataset is more relevant to our research question because it better reflects current social media habits. Although the 2023 dataset has some advantages in terms of sample size and participation, the more recent data is more useful for what we’re trying to study. Both datasets could help us identify relationships between social media use and certain behaviors, but we can’t necessarily conclude that social media directly causes those behaviors.
